name: Ahi
bio: Ahi, whose personal name was Hasan and who was popularly known as Befilu Hasan, 'Hasan with the Mole', was born in the village of Tirstinik near Nicopolis. He studied in Constantinople, became a Mulazim, and wrote ghazels from his student days. His makhlas, Ahi, means 'He of Sighs'. According to Katib Chelebi he died in Qara-Ferya, where he held a poor professorship, in A.H. 923 (1517–18).

Ahi began a romantic mesnevi on Khusrev and Shirin but abandoned it at the urging of a Naqshbendi sheykh, and left unfinished the ornate prose-and-verse allegory Husn u Dil ('Beauty and Heart'), together with a Diwan of ghazels. The Ottoman biographers rank him among the finest ghazel-writers of his day. Gibb translates two extracts from the Khusrev and Shirin and three of his ghazels.

poems.title: From the Khusrev u Shirin: Concerning the Birth of Khusrev
poems.author: Ahi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
It was as though one dawn the beldam Sphere
Had smirched the heav'nly skirt with bloody smear;
'T was e'en as Venus had delivered been,
And midst of blood had born the sun, I ween.
At dawn the Lady of the cycle bare
A boy with golden head, with yellow hair.
That Moon was born at happy fortune's rise;
'God aid him!' cried the angels from the skies.
In two weeks Khusrev grew to full moon fair;
A year, then as the Night of Power his hair.
His cypress on its foot began to stand,
And cooed the pheasant of his meadow-land.
Upon his rosebud-mouth there fell the dew,
And heart-sore for his cheek the tulip grew.

poems.title: From the Khusrev u Shirin: Concerning the Painting of the Portrait of Khusrev
poems.author: Ahi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
He showed him as he was, to nature true,
When Khusrev's picture like the sun he drew.
The black blood of the ink he grinded there,
And painted now his mole and now his hair.
When yonder form and figure 'gan arise
The Trumpet-pen caused resurrections rise.
With musky lines he drew his tresses rare;
He limned his waist with pencil of fine hair.
His lip was e'en that drop of blood thou'dst say
Wherein the Spirit Vital 's hid away.
When that sweet figure on the page was traced,
The Chinese picture blushed for shame, disgraced.
The Chinese idols' souls their bodies fled
When that bright cup, his mouth, was mentioned.
A myriad Chinese idols lifeless bode;
Amazed, their backs against the wall, they stood.
Pen-like, his head from 'fore it raised he, --
The artist washed his hands of artistry.

poems.title: Ghazel I
poems.author: Ahi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Let the clouds let loose their tresses, let the thunders moan and plain,
O'er my sepulchre till Doomsday let the tulips burn for pain.
'Tis the Sultan Rose's reign, so let the breezes dance and play;
At the beauty-cypress-tree's foot let the waters dew-drops rain.
So unhearted I for sickness in this dreary home of woe
That upon my mouth the moistened cotton 's laid by boil and blain.
For to write their teen and dule of soul who swallow blood and die
Doth the tulip's heart a page a-flame with glowing sparks contain.
Such the fires my sighs, O Ahi, have enkindled o'er their heads,
That through me this day have moan and groan their way to sky-ward ta'en.

poems.title: Ghazel II
poems.author: Ahi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Though I possess never a rush-mat in my hut of woe,
Yet on my bare skin do the mat-marks ever plainly show.
How doth the eye's pupil, ah me, deal by its children dear! --
I would them nurse here in my lap even as orphans, know.
Turning aside, there with the dogs haunting thy ward, I eat;
Ne'er have I seen friend o'mine yet bread and salt rights avow.
Unto me, Ahi, will it serve for my Deeds Register, --
So that there be in my Diwan lines on my dear, I trow.

poems.title: Ghazel III
poems.author: Ahi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
